result:
A race condition is when two processes touch shared state at the same time and the result depends on which one happens to run first, so it works most of the time and fails unpredictably. With a log file, the usual symptoms are interleaved or lost lines when two scripts write at once.

Wrap each write in `flock`, which makes writers take turns:

```sh
{
  flock 9
  echo "$(date -Is) job finished" >&9
} 9>>/var/log/shared.log
```

A single short `echo ... >> file` is already nearly safe, because `>>` opens the file in append mode and each small write lands at the end atomically on a local filesystem. You need the lock when one entry spans several writes, when lines are long (several KB), or when the file is on NFS, where append is not atomic and `flock` may itself be unreliable.

Never use `>` or a read-modify-write (read the file, edit, write it back) on a shared log: that is the classic race, and the second writer silently erases the first one's lines.
